newsitem.title: INDIA: India reforms seen resistant to political turmoil.
newsitem.headline: India reforms seen resistant to political turmoil.

text.p: India's economic reforms are safe and foreign investment is not likely to be affected by political instability, business leaders said on Sunday.
But the turmoil has placed a big question mark over some looming economic decisions, they said.

The crisis erupted after the Congress party, which provided crucial support to Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's centre-left coalition government, said it was pulling out and intended to stake its own claim to form a new government.
The Congress dropped its bombshell just a day before the unveiling of a five-year trade policy that is widely expected to sweep away a web of controls and free more imports.

"It will not affect the reforms process since all political parties are agreed on reforms," V. Raghuraman, the secretary general of Associated Chambers of Commerce and Industry (Assocham), told Reuters.
"We will have to wait and watch. Politics comes into focus and economics goes into background. There will be some uncertainty," Raghuraman said.
The business leaders said uncertainty must not linger.

Ahead of the government lay important decisions such as whether or not to raise the prices of petroleum products, the dilemma of domestic wheat procurement, and amendments to corporate laws, they said.
"In 1991 it was a minority government which introduced reforms," Amit Mitra, secretary of Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI), said.
He was referring to the launch six years ago of ambitious market-opening steps by a Congress government led by former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao.
"There was always a threat to that government, despite which reforms were initiated and intensified," Mitra said.
The immediate concern was parliamentary approval of the 1997/98 (April-March) federal budget, which has been widely hailed by domestic industry, brokers and business leaders said.
"We will have to see whether the budget will be passed," Assocham's Raghuraman said.
Shares on the country's premier Bombay bourse fell sharply in off-market kerb deals on Sunday on nervousness over the crisis.
Bombay's benchmark stocks index closed 72.05 points, or 1.9 percent lower, at 3663.53 on Friday.
"This is completely unanticipated," said the chief dealer at a London-based brokerage in Bombay. "I wouldn't be suprised if we see the index drop 200-300 points (on Monday)."
The flow of foreign direct investment into the economy is unlikely to be affected by political flux, analysts said.
"Why should it affect investor confidence. The economy has now acquired a momentum of its own," former finance minister and Congress leader Manmohan Singh told Reuters.
He said the world should by now recognise that political changes in India were a reality.

But the Confederation of Indian Industry said in a statement: "Political uncertainty at this juncture could slow down economic growth and erode the confidence of the foreign investor in India, and must be resolved quickly."
Commerce Minister Bolla Buli Ramaiah is scheduled to unveil the new trade policy on Monday. A Commerce Ministry spokeswoman said the announcement would not be affected by political changes.
In the end, business leaders said, they were optimistic India had reached a stage where economic policy-making was slowly gaining independence from the political system.
"Political instability or minority government process have in fact promoted reforms rather than distracted it," said Mitra.
